analysis.one_liner: Requires drug makers to rebate Medicaid so the program pays no more than any other big customer.
analysis.headline: Introduced by Sen. David Pryor with 4 Democratic cosponsors, the bill went only as far as referral to the Senate Finance Committee and never received a hearing, markup, or vote before the 101st Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required drug manufacturers to pay each state a quarterly rebate on Medicaid prescriptions so the program pays no more for brand-name drugs than the manufacturer's lowest price anywhere in the market, plus a 10% rebate on the average price of other drugs. In exchange, states could not exclude a compliant manufacturer's drugs from coverage, and the bill paired the money with pharmacist counseling requirements, protections for physicians' prescribing rights, and a share of rebates paid back to pharmacies. It never left the Senate Finance Committee before the 101st Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Medicaid beneficiaries — low-income seniors, people with disabilities, and poor families — whom the bill's findings say lose access to medications when states respond to drug price inflation by trimming drug coverage or raising copays; state taxpayers, who would recover the gap between what Medicaid pays and the best price drug makers give other large buyers; retail pharmacies, which would receive 10% of state rebates for 1991-1993, get annual dispensing-fee updates based on cost studies, and keep their reimbursement formula from being cut before March 1993; and physicians, whose prior-authorization requests would have to be answered immediately, 24 hours a day.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Medicaid patients, state budgets, and pharmacies

how_it_helps.text: Makes drug manufacturers pay states a quarterly rebate so that Medicaid ends up spending no more for single-source and brand-name multiple-source drugs than the manufacturer's best price charged to any other customer, and recovers 10% of the price on other drugs.

Bars states from using formularies or similar restrictions to exclude a manufacturer's drugs from coverage while the manufacturer pays rebates, so patients keep access to needed medications instead of states coping with price inflation by cutting drug lists or raising copays.

Requires pharmacists to review each prescription before it is filled and to offer counseling on how to use the medication, side effects, and interactions, with the federal government covering 75% of state drug-use-review costs.

Returns 10% of the rebates states collect to pharmacies for fiscal years 1991 through 1993, requires states to study the actual cost of dispensing prescriptions and update dispensing fees annually, and blocks reductions in pharmacist reimbursement formulas before March 1993.

Protects the physician's right to prescribe: state prior-approval programs may only operate if they respond immediately, 24 hours a day, and a doctor can obtain prior authorization for a drug from a manufacturer that refuses to pay rebates.

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name drug manufacturers, who would owe quarterly rebates equal to the gap between their average price and their best price, floored at 10% and capped at 25% of the price of units dispensed, plus penalties of up to $10,000 a day for late price reports and $100,000 per item of false price information; makers of other drugs, including generics, who would owe 10% of their average price; and manufacturers who tie drug purchases to their own monitoring services, which states could refuse to cover.

drawbacks.text: The 'best price' rule means Medicaid automatically gets the lowest price a manufacturer gives anyone, which gives the manufacturer a reason to stop offering deep discounts to hospitals, HMOs, and other buyers rather than let Medicaid match them — potentially raising prices for everyone outside Medicaid.

The compliance load is heavy: states must report utilization to every manufacturer within 60 days of each quarter, run prior-approval systems that answer around the clock, stand up physician-led drug review boards, and build point-of-sale electronic claims systems on fixed deadlines, with new federal matching funds covering part of the cost.
Prices reported by manufacturers and wholesalers would be kept confidential from public disclosure, so the public could not see what the government learned about drug pricing.

Savings are bounded by design: rebates cannot exceed 25% of the price of the drugs dispensed, and states are barred from restructuring pharmacist reimbursement to save money until March 1993, limiting state flexibility to cut their own costs.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill aims cost control at manufacturer prices rather than at benefits, and it is unusual in pairing the rebate with access protections — no formulary exclusions for paying manufacturers, pharmacy reimbursement floors, and physician prescribing rights — so the savings are not extracted from patients or providers. The real risks are indirect: the best-price definition could discourage manufacturers from discounting to other buyers, the reporting and review machinery is expensive to build, and confidentiality would keep manufacturer pricing data out of public view. On balance the trade is straightforward — an industry that gave large discounts to some customers but not to a publicly funded program for the poor would lose that discretion, and low-income patients and state budgets would gain.

outcome.mechanism: Introduced in the last weeks of the session, the bill was read twice and sent to the Senate Finance Committee, which never acted on it before the 101st Congress ended on January 3, 1991.

narrative.text: Sen. David Pryor introduced the bill on September 12, 1990; it was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Finance the same day, with four Democratic cosponsors joining.
Referral was the bill's last stop: the record shows no committee hearings, no markup, no committee vote, and no floor action of any kind.
The 101st Congress ended on January 3, 1991, and the bill expired in committee without ever coming to a vote.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Brand-name drug manufacturers were better off: the rebate requirement, the 10%-25% price band, and the penalties for false price reporting never took effect under this bill, and Medicaid kept paying prices above the discounts manufacturers gave other large buyers. No patient, pharmacy, or state gained anything from this bill because it never moved.

for.name: Sen. David Pryor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on September 12, 1990; it was read twice and referred to the Finance Committee the same day.

for.name: 4 of 55 Senate Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; no Republican signed on.

against.name: Senate Finance Committee
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after it was referred; no hearing, markup, or committee vote appears in the record.

against.name: Lloyd Bentsen
against.what_they_did: As committee chair, never scheduled consideration of the bill; it sat without action for the remainder of the session.

sides.party_line_note: All five Senate sponsors, including Pryor, were Democrats and no Republican cosponsored, but the bill never reached a vote, so there is no roll-call evidence of where the parties stood.

industries.note: The bill would force them to pay quarterly rebates ensuring Medicaid pays their best market price, within a 10%-25% band of the price of drugs dispensed, and imposes penalties for late or false price reporting; their business practice of discounting to large-volume buyers while declining similar terms to Medicaid is what the bill was written to end.
They would owe a flat rebate of 10% of their average price to wholesalers on units dispensed to Medicaid patients, a smaller but real cost on a thin-margin business.

Pharmacies would share 10% of state rebates for 1991-1993, get annual dispensing-fee updates based on cost studies, be protected from reimbursement-formula cuts until March 1993, and could be paid for drug review services under demonstration projects.

industries.industry: Health-care claims processing and telecommunications vendors
industries.note: States would be pushed to build point-of-sale electronic claims systems, with the federal government covering 90% of development and implementation costs in 1991-1992 through competitive procurement.
